own.claim: A meeting request with two specific times offered is the easiest ask to answer: it requires only a one-line reply and costs nothing to grant.
own.why: The counterparty has done the work of finding times; you need only pick one. Delay on this kind of ask is disproportionately costly to the relationship.

own.claim: When a counterparty you do not yet know proposes a meeting and you do not reply within a day, they assume you are not interested and move on.
own.why: A meeting request is a low-friction ask; a slow reply signals that the meeting is not a priority, which the counterparty reads as low interest in them.

own.claim: The reason for a meeting should be known before you confirm the time, or the meeting will be awkward and may waste both parties' time.
own.why: If you do not know why Brightloop wants to meet, you cannot prepare, and the meeting may be a mismatch of expectations.

patterns.claim: A counterparty who proposes specific meeting times and asks for confirmation before sending an invite is signalling genuine interest and expects a prompt reply.
Silence on a meeting proposal for over three days, when the proposed dates are imminent, reads as either disinterest or disorganisation and risks the counterparty withdrawing the offer.
Administrative silence from a counterparty is usually process, not sentiment; but silence from the founder on a meeting request is usually read as a signal.

scenarios.act: You confirm one of the two meeting times, Sana sends the invite, and the meeting happens as scheduled. You learn what Brightloop wants and can decide whether to pursue the relationship.
